custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__dict__, obj=mappingproxy({'__module__': 'simplebench._pytest', '__doc__': "\n    A callable object provided by the `benchmark` fixture to register a benchmark case.\n\n    The only REQUIRED parameter is `action`.\n\n    :param benchmark_id: An optional unique identifier for the benchmark case.\n\n        If None, a transient ID is assigned. This is meant to provide a stable identifier for the\n        benchmark case across multiple runs for tracking purposes. If not provided,\n        an attempt will be made to generate a stable ID based on the the action function\n        name, signature, and group. If that is not possible, a transient ID based\n        on the instance's id() will be used. If a transient ID is used, it will differ\n        between runs and cannot be used to correlate results across multiple runs.\n\n        Benchmark ids must be unique within a benchmarking session and stable across runs\n        or they cannot be used for tracking benchmark results over time.\n    :param vcs_info: An optional VCSInfo instance representing the state of the VCS repository.\n\n        If not provided, the VCSInfo will be automatically retrieved from the current\n        context of the caller if the code is part of a supported VCS repository.\n    :param action: The function to perform the benchmark.\n\n        This function must accept a `bench` instance of type SimpleRunner and\n        arbitrary keyword arguments ('**kwargs'). See the ``ActionRunner``\n        protocol for the exact signature required. It must return a `Results` object.\n    :param group: The benchmark reporting group to which the benchmark case belongs.\n\n        Benchmarks with the same group can be selected for execution without running\n        other benchmarks. If not specified, the default group 'default' is used.\n    :param title: The title of the benchmark case.\n\n        If None, the name of the action function will be used. Cannot be blank.\n    :param description: A brief description of the benchmark case.\n\n        If None, the docstring of the action function will be used, or\n        '(no description)' if no docstring is available. custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="\n    A benchmark case defines the specific benchmark to be run, including the\n    action to be performed, the parameters for the benchmark, and any variations\n    of those parameters as well as the reporting group and title for the benchmark.\n\n    It also defines the number of iterations, warmup iterations, rounds, minimum and maximum\n    time for the benchmark, the benchmark runner to use, and any callbacks to be invoked\n    to process the results of the benchmark for reporting purposes.\n\n    The min_time, max_time, iterations, and warmup_iterations parameters control how\n    the benchmark is executed and measured and interact with each other as follows when\n    using the default SimpleRunner:\n    - The benchmark will perform `warmup_iterations` iterations before starting the timing\n        and measurement phase. This is done to allow for any setup or caching effects to stabilize.\n        This is separate from the main benchmark iterations and does not count towards the\n        `iterations` count or the `min_time`/`max_time` limits.\n    - The benchmark will run for at least `min_time` wall clock seconds, but will stop on\n        completing the first iteration that ends after `max_time` seconds during the timing phase.\n    - If the benchmark completes `iterations` iterations after `min_time` but before\n        reaching `max_time`, it will stop.\n\n    This means that the benchmark will run for at least `min_time` seconds and\n    for at least one iteration during the timing phase. If `min_time` is reached\n    before `iterations` is completed, the benchmark will continue running until\n    either `iterations` or `max_time` is completed (whichever happens first).\n\n    `rounds` specifies the number of times the action will be executed per iteration to get a better average.\n    Each iteration will run the specified number of rounds after setup and before teardown. The timing\n    for the iteration will be the average time taken for the rounds in that iteration.\n\n    This helps to reduce the impact of variability in execution time for a single run of the action\n    for very fast actions. This suppresses the overhead of the loop and timer quantization in Python\n    during the actual timing benchmark/measurement phase. Internally, the action is called `rounds` times\n    in an unrolled loop for each iteration, and the average time per call is used for the iteration timing.\n\n    This removes the overhead of the loop and timer quantization in Python during the actual timing\n    benchmark/measurement phase by aggregating multiple calls to the action within a single iteration\n    without the overhead of looping constructs. This allows for more accurate timing of very fast actions\n    by reducing the relative impact of loop overhead and timer resolution limitations.\n\n    The trade-off is that total number of action calls is now `iterations * rounds`, and\n    the reported time per action call is an average over the rounds in each iteration. This can\n    dramatically improve the accuracy of timing measurements for very fast actions, at the cost\n    of increased total execution time for the benchmark due to the additional calls to the action.\n\n    The unrolled loop means that setup and teardown functions (if any) are called only once per iteration,\n    not once per round. All rounds in the same iteration share the same setup/teardown context.\n\n    It is recommended to leave `rounds` to its default of ``None``. A setting of ``None`` enables\n    auto-calibration of rounds based on the expected execution time of the action and the\n    precision and overhead of the timer function. If you do use it, you may want to run dual benchmarks\n    with `rounds=1` and `rounds >> 1` to see how much the reported variability and other metrics change.\n\n    The Case class is designed to be immutable after creation. Once a Case instance\n    is created, its properties cannot be directly changed. This immutability ensures that\n    benchmark cases remain consistent throughout their lifecycle.\n\n    The results of the benchmark runs are stored in the `results` property, which is a list\n    of Results objects. Each Results object corresponds to a specific combination of\n    keyword argument variations.\n\n    .. code-block:: python3\n      :caption: Minimal Example\n\n        from simplebench import (\n            Case, BenchmarkRunner, Results, main)\n\n\n        def my_benchmark_action(bench: BenchmarkRunner,\n                                **kwargs) -> Results:\n            # Perform benchmark action here\n            def benchmark_operation():\n                sum(range(1000))  # Example operation to benchmark\n\n            return bench.run(benchmark_operation)\n\n\n        if __name__ == '__main__':\n            cases_list: list[Case] = [\n                Case(action=my_benchmark_action)\n            ]\n            main(cases_list)\n\n    ", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="\n    A benchmark case defines the specific benchmark to be run, including the\n    action to be performed, the parameters for the benchmark, and any variations\n    of those parameters as well as the reporting group and title for the benchmark.\n\n    It also defines the number of iterations, warmup iterations, rounds, minimum and maximum\n    time for the benchmark, the benchmark runner to use, and any callbacks to be invoked\n    to process the results of the benchmark for reporting purposes.\n\n    The min_time, max_time, iterations, and warmup_iterations parameters control how\n    the benchmark is executed and measured and interact with each other as follows when\n    using the default SimpleRunner:\n    - The benchmark will perform `warmup_iterations` iterations before starting the timing\n        and measurement phase. This is done to allow for any setup or caching effects to stabilize.\n        This is separate from the main benchmark iterations and does not count towards the\n        `iterations` count or the `min_time`/`max_time` limits.\n    - The benchmark will run for at least `min_time` wall clock seconds, but will stop on\n        completing the first iteration that ends after `max_time` seconds during the timing phase.\n    - If the benchmark completes `iterations` iterations after `min_time` but before\n        reaching `max_time`, it will stop.\n\n    This means that the benchmark will run for at least `min_time` seconds and\n    for at least one iteration during the timing phase. If `min_time` is reached\n    before `iterations` is completed, the benchmark will continue running until\n    either `iterations` or `max_time` is completed (whichever happens first).\n\n    `rounds` specifies the number of times the action will be executed per iteration to get a better average.\n    Each iteration will run the specified number of rounds after setup and before teardown. The timing\n    for the iteration will be the average time taken for the rounds in that iteration.\n\n    This helps to reduce the impact of variability in execution time for a single run of the action\n    for very fast actions. This suppresses the overhead of the loop and timer quantization in Python\n    during the actual timing benchmark/measurement phase. Internally, the action is called `rounds` times\n    in an unrolled loop for each iteration, and the average time per call is used for the iteration timing.\n\n    This removes the overhead of the loop and timer quantization in Python during the actual timing\n    benchmark/measurement phase by aggregating multiple calls to the action within a single iteration\n    without the overhead of looping constructs. This allows for more accurate timing of very fast actions\n    by reducing the relative impact of loop overhead and timer resolution limitations.\n\n    The trade-off is that total number of action calls is now `iterations * rounds`, and\n    the reported time per action call is an average over the rounds in each iteration. This can\n    dramatically improve the accuracy of timing measurements for very fast actions, at the cost\n    of increased total execution time for the benchmark due to the additional calls to the action.\n\n    The unrolled loop means that setup and teardown functions (if any) are called only once per iteration,\n    not once per round. All rounds in the same iteration share the same setup/teardown context.\n\n    It is recommended to leave `rounds` to its default of ``None``. A setting of ``None`` enables\n    auto-calibration of rounds based on the expected execution time of the action and the\n    precision and overhead of the timer function. If you do use it, you may want to run dual benchmarks\n    with `rounds=1` and `rounds >> 1` to see how much the reported variability and other metrics change.\n\n    The Case class is designed to be immutable after creation. Once a Case instance\n    is created, its properties cannot be directly changed. This immutability ensures that\n    benchmark cases remain consistent throughout their lifecycle.\n\n    The results of the benchmark runs are stored in the `results` property, which is a list\n    of Results objects. Each Results object corresponds to a specific combination of\n    keyword argument variations.\n\n    .. code-block:: python3\n      :caption: Minimal Example\n\n        from simplebench import (\n            Case, BenchmarkRunner, Results, main)\n\n\n        def my_benchmark_action(bench: BenchmarkRunner,\n                                **kwargs) -> Results:\n            # Perform benchmark action here\n            def benchmark_operation():\n                sum(range(1000))  # Example operation to benchmark\n\n            return bench.run(benchmark_operation)\n\n\n        if __name__ == '__main__':\n            cases_list: list[Case] = [\n                Case(action=my_benchmark_action)\n            ]\n            main(cases_list)\n\n    ", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="\n    A benchmark case defines the specific benchmark to be run, including the\n    action to be performed, the parameters for the benchmark, and any variations\n    of those parameters as well as the reporting group and title for the benchmark.\n\n    It also defines the number of iterations, warmup iterations, rounds, minimum and maximum\n    time for the benchmark, the benchmark runner to use, and any callbacks to be invoked\n    to process the results of the benchmark for reporting purposes.\n\n    The min_time, max_time, iterations, and warmup_iterations parameters control how\n    the benchmark is executed and measured and interact with each other as follows when\n    using the default SimpleRunner:\n    - The benchmark will perform `warmup_iterations` iterations before starting the timing\n        and measurement phase. This is done to allow for any setup or caching effects to stabilize.\n        This is separate from the main benchmark iterations and does not count towards the\n        `iterations` count or the `min_time`/`max_time` limits.\n    - The benchmark will run for at least `min_time` wall clock seconds, but will stop on\n        completing the first iteration that ends after `max_time` seconds during the timing phase.\n    - If the benchmark completes `iterations` iterations after `min_time` but before\n        reaching `max_time`, it will stop.\n\n    This means that the benchmark will run for at least `min_time` seconds and\n    for at least one iteration during the timing phase. If `min_time` is reached\n    before `iterations` is completed, the benchmark will continue running until\n    either `iterations` or `max_time` is completed (whichever happens first).\n\n    `rounds` specifies the number of times the action will be executed per iteration to get a better average.\n    Each iteration will run the specified number of rounds after setup and before teardown. The timing\n    for the iteration will be the average time taken for the rounds in that iteration.\n\n    This helps to reduce the impact of variability in execution time for a single run of the action\n    for very fast actions. This suppresses the overhead of the loop and timer quantization in Python\n    during the actual timing benchmark/measurement phase. Internally, the action is called `rounds` times\n    in an unrolled loop for each iteration, and the average time per call is used for the iteration timing.\n\n    This removes the overhead of the loop and timer quantization in Python during the actual timing\n    benchmark/measurement phase by aggregating multiple calls to the action within a single iteration\n    without the overhead of looping constructs. This allows for more accurate timing of very fast actions\n    by reducing the relative impact of loop overhead and timer resolution limitations.\n\n    The trade-off is that total number of action calls is now `iterations * rounds`, and\n    the reported time per action call is an average over the rounds in each iteration. This can\n    dramatically improve the accuracy of timing measurements for very fast actions, at the cost\n    of increased total execution time for the benchmark due to the additional calls to the action.\n\n    The unrolled loop means that setup and teardown functions (if any) are called only once per iteration,\n    not once per round. All rounds in the same iteration share the same setup/teardown context.\n\n    It is recommended to leave `rounds` to its default of ``None``. A setting of ``None`` enables\n    auto-calibration of rounds based on the expected execution time of the action and the\n    precision and overhead of the timer function. If you do use it, you may want to run dual benchmarks\n    with `rounds=1` and `rounds >> 1` to see how much the reported variability and other metrics change.\n\n    The Case class is designed to be immutable after creation. Once a Case instance\n    is created, its properties cannot be directly changed. This immutability ensures that\n    benchmark cases remain consistent throughout their lifecycle.\n\n    The results of the benchmark runs are stored in the `results` property, which is a list\n    of Results objects. Each Results object corresponds to a specific combination of\n    keyword argument variations.\n\n    .. code-block:: python3\n      :caption: Minimal Example\n\n        from simplebench import (\n            Case, BenchmarkRunner, Results, main)\n\n\n        def my_benchmark_action(bench: BenchmarkRunner,\n                                **kwargs) -> Results:\n            # Perform benchmark action here\n            def benchmark_operation():\n                sum(range(1000))  # Example operation to benchmark\n\n            return bench.run(benchmark_operation)\n\n\n        if __name__ == '__main__':\n            cases_list: list[Case] = [\n                Case(action=my_benchmark_action)\n            ]\n            main(cases_list)\n\n    ", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="Create a PythonInfo facade for the Python :module:`platform` functions.\n\n    It is a typed object-oriented representation of the Python environment\n    where it was created and cleanly exposes the following :module:`platform`\n    derived information. It is NOT a direct mapping of :module:`platform` functions,\n    but rather a higher-level abstraction that provides the following properties\n    after gathering and processing the relevant data to account for different\n    Python implementations:\n\n    - `version` - version number of the Python interpreter.\n    - `implementation` - name of the Python implementation.\n    - `implementation_version` - version of the Python implementation.\n    - `compiler` - compiler used to build the Python interpreter.\n    - `revision` - revision of the Python implementation.\n    - `buildno` - build number of the Python interpreter.\n    - `builddate` - build date of the Python interpreter.\n    - `command_line_flags` - command line flags used to start the interpreter.\n    - `environment_variables` - Python-specific environment variables that are set.\n\n    It unpacks the :func:`platform.python_build()` tuple into separate string attributes for easier\n    access and type casts :func:`platform.python_version()` to a string for static typing tools\n    because there is no type hint for it in the :module:`platform` module and static analysis tools\n    sometimes get confused by it.\n\n    It also inspects :attr:`sys.flags` to construct a string representation of the command line flags\n    used to start the interpreter and gathers a read-only mapping of Python-specific environment variables\n    that are set in the current environment. Both of the are sorted for consistency in\n    representation and comparison.\n\n    By 'snapshotting' this information at initialization, the PythonInfo class provides\n    a consistent view of the Python environment that can be easily passed around and used\n    in other parts of the application or reporting tools and makes it possible to\n    serialize (such as by pickling) this information if needed.\n    ", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="Create a PythonInfo facade for the Python :module:`platform` functions.\n\n    It is a typed object-oriented representation of the Python environment\n    where it was created and cleanly exposes the following :module:`platform`\n    derived information. It is NOT a direct mapping of :module:`platform` functions,\n    but rather a higher-level abstraction that provides the following properties\n    after gathering and processing the relevant data to account for different\n    Python implementations:\n\n    - `version` - version number of the Python interpreter.\n    - `implementation` - name of the Python implementation.\n    - `implementation_version` - version of the Python implementation.\n    - `compiler` - compiler used to build the Python interpreter.\n    - `revision` - revision of the Python implementation.\n    - `buildno` - build number of the Python interpreter.\n    - `builddate` - build date of the Python interpreter.\n    - `command_line_flags` - command line flags used to start the interpreter.\n    - `environment_variables` - Python-specific environment variables that are set.\n\n    It unpacks the :func:`platform.python_build()` tuple into separate string attributes for easier\n    access and type casts :func:`platform.python_version()` to a string for static typing tools\n    because there is no type hint for it in the :module:`platform` module and static analysis tools\n    sometimes get confused by it.\n\n    It also inspects :attr:`sys.flags` to construct a string representation of the command line flags\n    used to start the interpreter and gathers a read-only mapping of Python-specific environment variables\n    that are set in the current environment. Both of the are sorted for consistency in\n    representation and comparison.\n\n    By 'snapshotting' this information at initialization, the PythonInfo class provides\n    a consistent view of the Python environment that can be easily passed around and used\n    in other parts of the application or reporting tools and makes it possible to\n    serialize (such as by pickling) this information if needed.\n    ", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

and benchmarks.\n\nThis is used by reporters to specify what the metric types of benchmark results are.\n\nDefined Metric Types are:\n\n- `STD_OPS_STATS`: Operations per second metric statistics.\n- `STD_OPS_RAW`: Raw list of operations per second data.\n- `STD_TIMING_STATS`: Time per measurement metric statistics.\n- `STD_TIMING_RAW`: Raw list of time per measurement data.\n- `STD_MEMORY_STATS`: Memory usage metric statistics.\n- `STD_MEMORY_RAW`: Raw list of memory usage data.\n- `STD_PEAK_MEMORY_STATS`: Peak memory usage metric statistics.\n- `STD_PEAK_MEMORY_RAW`: Raw list of peak memory usage data metric.\n- `STD_TOTAL_ELAPSED_TIME`: Total elapsed time for the benchmark.\n- `STD_TOTAL_CPU_TIME`: Total CPU time for the benchmark.\n- `STD_CPU_TIME_STATS`: CPU time per measurement metric statistics.\n- `STD_CPU_TIME_RAW`: Raw list of CPU time per measurement data.\n- `STD_GC_GEN0_COLLECTIONS_STATS`: Number of garbage collections for generation 0\n- `STD_GC_GEN0_COLLECTIONS_RAW`: Number of garbage collections for generation 0 (raw values)\n- `STD_GC_GEN1_COLLECTIONS_STATS`: Number of garbage collections for generation 1\n- `STD_GC_GEN1_COLLECTIONS_RAW`: Number of garbage collections for generation 1 (raw values)\n- `STD_GC_GEN2_COLLECTIONS_STATS`: Number of garbage collections for generation 2\n- `STD_GC_GEN2_COLLECTIONS_RAW`: Number of garbage collections for generation 2 (raw values)\n- `STD_GC_GEN0_COLLECTED_STATS`: Number of objects collected by garbage collection for generation 0\n- `STD_GC_GEN0_COLLECTED_RAW`: Number of objects collected by garbage collection for generation 0 (raw values)\n- `STD_GC_GEN1_COLLECTED_STATS`: Number of objects collected by garbage collection for generation 1\n- `STD_GC_GEN1_COLLECTED_RAW`: Number of objects collected by garbage collection for generation 1 (raw values)\n- `STD_GC_GEN2_COLLECTED_STATS`: Number of objects collected by garbage collection for generation 2\n- `STD_GC_GEN2_COLLECTED_RAW`: Number of objects collected by garbage collection for generation 2 (raw values)\n- `STD_GC_GEN0_UNCOLLECTABLE_STATS`: Number of uncollectable objects for generation 0\n- `STD_GC_GEN0_UNCOLLECTABLE_RAW`: Number of uncollectable objects for generation 0 (raw values)\n- `STD_GC_GEN1_UNCOLLECTABLE_STATS`: Number of uncollectable objects for generation 1\n- `STD_GC_GEN1_UNCOLLECTABLE_RAW`: Number of uncollectable objects for generation 1 (raw values)\n- `STD_GC_GEN2_UNCOLLECTABLE_STATS`: Number of uncollectable objects for generation 2\n- `STD_GC_GEN2_UNCOLLECTABLE_RAW`: Number of uncollectable objects for generation 2 (raw values)\nThe 'STD_' prefix is used to indicate that the metric is a standard metric type\ndefined by the SimpleBench library. Custom metric types should use a different prefix.\nIdeally, custom metric types should use a prefix that is unique to the benchmark or\nbenchmark suite that defines them to avoid conflicts with other metric types.\n\nAlthough metric types are primarily identified by their semantic type,\nhaving standard labels and units helps with readability, selectability, and consistency\nacross different benchmarks and reporters and allows for specification of metrics\nin a standardized way.\n\nTo promote reusability and consistency, it is advisable to use these standard metric types\nwhenever applicable, especially for common metrics like operations per second and timing.\n\nIf a metric type does not fit any of the standard types defined here,\na custom metric type should be created with a unique semantic type\nto avoid conflicts with existing types.\n\nMetric types and actual metrics are split into two separate concepts:\n- Metric Types define the nature of the measurement (e.g., operations per second).\n- Metrics are instances that use these types to represent specific measurements\n    in benchmarks (e.g., STD_OPS metric using STD_OPS metric type).\n\nMultiple metrics can share the same metric type if they represent similar measurements\nbut differ in other attributes like labels or descriptions because they are used\nin different contexts.\n", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=module, name=__doc__, obj='V1 StatsBlock class\n\nThis class represents a stats block information in a JSON report.\n\nIt implements validation and serialization/deserialization methods to and from dictionaries\nfor the following JSON Schema version:\n\nhttps://raw.githubusercontent.com/JerilynFranz/python-simplebench/main/schemas/v1/stats-block.json\n\nIt is the base implemention of the JSON report stats block representation.\n\nThis makes the implementations of StatsBlock backwards compatible with future versions\nof the JSON report schema and the V1 implementation itself is essentially a frozen snapshot\nof the base CPUInfo representation at the time of the V1 schema release.\n\nThe code has three basic paths for creating a stats block:\n\n1. Creation by directly instantiating the `StatsBlock` class with the required statistical parameters.\n2. Creation by instantiating the `StatsBlock` class with the raw data measurements and\n   having the class calculate the statistical parameters.\n3. Creation by using the `from_dict` class method to create a `StatsBlock` instance from a\n   dictionary that matches the JSON schema.\n\nThe created instance and all values available via properties are immutable once created\nand can be serialized back to a dictionary using the `to_dict` method.\n\nThe class also implements equality and hashing methods to allow comparison\nand use in hash-based collections like sets and dictionaries. It also\nimplements size-optimized pickling support for serialization/deserialization.\n\nThe dictionary serialized representation matches the JSON schema for version 1 reports\nand can be used for JSON serialization and deserialization.\n', skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__dict__, obj=mappingproxy({'__module__': 'simplebench.reporters.choice.choice', '__doc__': "Definition of a :class:`~.Choice` option for live use by reporters.\n\n    A :class:`~.Choice` represents a specific configuration of a\n    :class:`~simplebench.reporters.reporter.Reporter` subclass,\n    including the metrics to include in the report,\n    the output targets, and the output formats.\n\n    The :class:`~.Choice` class provides a structured way to define and manage\n    different reporting options within the SimpleBench framework so that\n    users can select from predefined configurations and developers can\n    easily add new reporting options to the framework.\n\n    A :class:`~.Choice` instance is immutable after creation to ensure consistency\n    in reporting configurations.\n\n    The metrics, targets, and formats are descriptive only; they do not\n    enforce any behavior on the associated :class:`~simplebench.reporters.reporter.Reporter`\n    subclass. Default includes\n        FILESYSTEM, CONSOLE, and CALLBACK.\n    :ivar default_targets: The default output target if none is specified. custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="Class for holding MatPlotLib graph reporter specific options.\n\n    This class extends the :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.options.GraphOptions`\n    interface and forms a new interface for options specific to MatPlotLib-based\n    graph reporters.\n\n    It makes it easy to create graph reporters with MatPlotLib by providing\n    a standard set of options that can be used across multiple reporters via\n    subclassing.\n\n    It includes the defaults for various MatPlotLib reporter defaults that can be\n    set globally for all MatPlotLib reporters via static methods, as well as instance-specific\n    options that can be set when creating a :class:`~.MatPlotLibOptions` instance or when creating\n    a benchmark test case.\n\n    The philosophy behind having both static/global defaults and instance-specific options\n    is to provide flexibility in configuration in a 'simple things should be simple, complex\n    things should be possible' manner.\n\n    Users can set global defaults that apply to all MatPlotLib reporters, ensuring easy\n    consistency across reports. At the same time, instance-specific options allow\n    for customization on a per-report basis, enabling users to tailor the behavior of\n    individual reports as needed.\n\n    The baseline defaults provided here are intended to offer a good balance between\n    quality, appearance, and performance for most common use cases.\n\n    Those defaults are as follows:\n        - Width: ``1500`` pixels\n        - Height: ``750`` pixels\n        - DPI: ``150``\n        - Y-axis starts at zero: ``True``\n        - X-axis labels rotation: ``45.0`` degrees\n        - Style: :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.enums.style.Style.DARK_BACKGROUND`\n        - Theme: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.theme.DefaultTheme`\n        - ImageType: :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.enums.image_type.ImageType.SVG`\n\n        These defaults are used both by :class:`~simplebench.case.Case` instances when\n        creating reports for specific test cases and by\n        :class:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice` instances when creating reports\n        for all test cases under that :class:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice`.\n\n        The semantics are that :attr:`~simplebench.case.Case.options` take precedence over\n        :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice.options` take precedence\n        over the class defaults. custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="Class for holding MatPlotLib graph reporter specific options.\n\n    This class extends the :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.options.GraphOptions`\n    interface and forms a new interface for options specific to MatPlotLib-based\n    graph reporters.\n\n    It makes it easy to create graph reporters with MatPlotLib by providing\n    a standard set of options that can be used across multiple reporters via\n    subclassing.\n\n    It includes the defaults for various MatPlotLib reporter defaults that can be\n    set globally for all MatPlotLib reporters via static methods, as well as instance-specific\n    options that can be set when creating a :class:`~.MatPlotLibOptions` instance or when creating\n    a benchmark test case.\n\n    The philosophy behind having both static/global defaults and instance-specific options\n    is to provide flexibility in configuration in a 'simple things should be simple, complex\n    things should be possible' manner.\n\n    Users can set global defaults that apply to all MatPlotLib reporters, ensuring easy\n    consistency across reports. At the same time, instance-specific options allow\n    for customization on a per-report basis, enabling users to tailor the behavior of\n    individual reports as needed.\n\n    The baseline defaults provided here are intended to offer a good balance between\n    quality, appearance, and performance for most common use cases.\n\n    Those defaults are as follows:\n        - Width: ``1500`` pixels\n        - Height: ``750`` pixels\n        - DPI: ``150``\n        - Y-axis starts at zero: ``True``\n        - X-axis labels rotation: ``45.0`` degrees\n        - Style: :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.enums.style.Style.DARK_BACKGROUND`\n        - Theme: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.theme.DefaultTheme`\n        - ImageType: :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.enums.image_type.ImageType.SVG`\n\n        These defaults are used both by :class:`~simplebench.case.Case` instances when\n        creating reports for specific test cases and by\n        :class:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice` instances when creating reports\n        for all test cases under that :class:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice`.\n\n        The semantics are that :attr:`~simplebench.case.Case.options` take precedence over\n        :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice.options` take precedence\n        over the class defaults. This allows for flexible configuration at multiple levels.\n\n    :ivar width: The default width of the MatPlotLib output in pixels when rendered.\n    :vartype width: int\n    :ivar height: The default height of the MatPlotLib output in pixels when rendered.\n    :vartype height: int\n    :ivar dpi: The default DPI (dots per inch) for the MatPlotLib output when rendered.\n    :vartype dpi: int\n    :ivar y_starts_at_zero: The default for whether the Y-axis for graphs should start at zero.\n    :vartype y_starts_at_zero: bool\n    :ivar x_labels_rotation: The default rotation angle in degrees for X-axis labels.\n    :vartype x_labels_rotation: float\n    :ivar style: The default style for the MatPlotLib graphs.\n    :vartype style: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.enums.style.Style`\n    :ivar theme: The default theme to use for the MatPlotLib graphs.\n    :vartype theme: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.theme.Theme`\n    :ivar image_type: The output image format for the graph files.\n    :vartype image_type: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.enums.image_type.ImageType`\n    ", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="Class for holding MatPlotLib graph reporter specific options.\n\n    This class extends the :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.options.GraphOptions`\n    interface and forms a new interface for options specific to MatPlotLib-based\n    graph reporters.\n\n    It makes it easy to create graph reporters with MatPlotLib by providing\n    a standard set of options that can be used across multiple reporters via\n    subclassing.\n\n    It includes the defaults for various MatPlotLib reporter defaults that can be\n    set globally for all MatPlotLib reporters via static methods, as well as instance-specific\n    options that can be set when creating a :class:`~.MatPlotLibOptions` instance or when creating\n    a benchmark test case.\n\n    The philosophy behind having both static/global defaults and instance-specific options\n    is to provide flexibility in configuration in a 'simple things should be simple, complex\n    things should be possible' manner.\n\n    Users can set global defaults that apply to all MatPlotLib reporters, ensuring easy\n    consistency across reports. At the same time, instance-specific options allow\n    for customization on a per-report basis, enabling users to tailor the behavior of\n    individual reports as needed.\n\n    The baseline defaults provided here are intended to offer a good balance between\n    quality, appearance, and performance for most common use cases.\n\n    Those defaults are as follows:\n        - Width: ``1500`` pixels\n        - Height: ``750`` pixels\n        - DPI: ``150``\n        - Y-axis starts at zero: ``True``\n        - X-axis labels rotation: ``45.0`` degrees\n        - Style: :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.enums.style.Style.DARK_BACKGROUND`\n        - Theme: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.theme.DefaultTheme`\n        - ImageType: :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.enums.image_type.ImageType.SVG`\n\n        These defaults are used both by :class:`~simplebench.case.Case` instances when\n        creating reports for specific test cases and by\n        :class:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice` instances when creating reports\n        for all test cases under that :class:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice`.\n\n        The semantics are that :attr:`~simplebench.case.Case.options` take precedence over\n        :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice.options` take precedence\n        over the class defaults. This allows for flexible configuration at multiple levels.\n\n    :ivar width: The default width of the MatPlotLib output in pixels when rendered.\n    :vartype width: int\n    :ivar height: The default height of the MatPlotLib output in pixels when rendered.\n    :vartype height: int\n    :ivar dpi: The default DPI (dots per inch) for the MatPlotLib output when rendered.\n    :vartype dpi: int\n    :ivar y_starts_at_zero: The default for whether the Y-axis for graphs should start at zero.\n    :vartype y_starts_at_zero: bool\n    :ivar x_labels_rotation: The default rotation angle in degrees for X-axis labels.\n    :vartype x_labels_rotation: float\n    :ivar style: The default style for the MatPlotLib graphs.\n    :vartype style: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.enums.style.Style`\n    :ivar theme: The default theme to use for the MatPlotLib graphs.\n    :vartype theme: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.theme.Theme`\n    :ivar image_type: The output image format for the graph files.\n    :vartype image_type: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.enums.image_type.ImageType`\n    ", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

custom_skip_member called: app=<class 'sphinx.application.Sphinx'>, what=class, name=__doc__, obj="Class for holding MatPlotLib graph reporter specific options.\n\n    This class extends the :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.options.GraphOptions`\n    interface and forms a new interface for options specific to MatPlotLib-based\n    graph reporters.\n\n    It makes it easy to create graph reporters with MatPlotLib by providing\n    a standard set of options that can be used across multiple reporters via\n    subclassing.\n\n    It includes the defaults for various MatPlotLib reporter defaults that can be\n    set globally for all MatPlotLib reporters via static methods, as well as instance-specific\n    options that can be set when creating a :class:`~.MatPlotLibOptions` instance or when creating\n    a benchmark test case.\n\n    The philosophy behind having both static/global defaults and instance-specific options\n    is to provide flexibility in configuration in a 'simple things should be simple, complex\n    things should be possible' manner.\n\n    Users can set global defaults that apply to all MatPlotLib reporters, ensuring easy\n    consistency across reports. At the same time, instance-specific options allow\n    for customization on a per-report basis, enabling users to tailor the behavior of\n    individual reports as needed.\n\n    The baseline defaults provided here are intended to offer a good balance between\n    quality, appearance, and performance for most common use cases.\n\n    Those defaults are as follows:\n        - Width: ``1500`` pixels\n        - Height: ``750`` pixels\n        - DPI: ``150``\n        - Y-axis starts at zero: ``True``\n        - X-axis labels rotation: ``45.0`` degrees\n        - Style: :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.enums.style.Style.DARK_BACKGROUND`\n        - Theme: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.theme.DefaultTheme`\n        - ImageType: :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.enums.image_type.ImageType.SVG`\n\n        These defaults are used both by :class:`~simplebench.case.Case` instances when\n        creating reports for specific test cases and by\n        :class:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice` instances when creating reports\n        for all test cases under that :class:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice`.\n\n        The semantics are that :attr:`~simplebench.case.Case.options` take precedence over\n        :attr:`~simplebench.reporters.choice.Choice.options` take precedence\n        over the class defaults. This allows for flexible configuration at multiple levels.\n\n    :ivar width: The default width of the MatPlotLib output in pixels when rendered.\n    :vartype width: int\n    :ivar height: The default height of the MatPlotLib output in pixels when rendered.\n    :vartype height: int\n    :ivar dpi: The default DPI (dots per inch) for the MatPlotLib output when rendered.\n    :vartype dpi: int\n    :ivar y_starts_at_zero: The default for whether the Y-axis for graphs should start at zero.\n    :vartype y_starts_at_zero: bool\n    :ivar x_labels_rotation: The default rotation angle in degrees for X-axis labels.\n    :vartype x_labels_rotation: float\n    :ivar style: The default style for the MatPlotLib graphs.\n    :vartype style: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.enums.style.Style`\n    :ivar theme: The default theme to use for the MatPlotLib graphs.\n    :vartype theme: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.matplotlib.theme.Theme`\n    :ivar image_type: The output image format for the graph files.\n    :vartype image_type: :class:`~simplebench.reporters.graph.enums.image_type.ImageType`\n    ", skip=True, options=<class 'sphinx.ext.autodoc.Options'>

If ``None``, no width constraint is applied.\n\n        The virtual width is used to determine how the table should be formatted when\n        rendered to non-console outputs, such as files or callbacks. This allows for\n        better control over the appearance of the table in different contexts.\n    :param fields: A tuple of Rich Table fields to include in the output.\n        If none is specifically set, a predefined set of fields is used.
